facts.text: On 3 October 1994 Rehib Çabuk and Sefer Cerf were killed in Adana. They were, respectively, district leader and administrative board member of HADEP, a pro-Kurdish political party.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  On 3 October 1994 Rehib Çabuk and Sefer Cerf were killed in Adana. They were, respectively, district leader and administrative board member of HADEP (Halkın Demokrasi Partisi, People’s Democracy Party), a pro-Kurdish political party.

facts.text: The applicant witnessed the killing and attended the funeral on 4 October 1994.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant witnessed the killing and attended the funeral on 4 October 1994.

facts.text: On 5 October 1994, at about 11 a.m., two persons identifying themselves as policemen from the anti-terrorism branch entered the Erzurumlular Café in Adana and told the applicant to come out.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On 5 October 1994, at about 11 a.m., while the applicant was sitting in the Erzurumlular Café in the Mutlu neighbourhood in Adana, two persons, who later identified themselves as policemen, entered the café.

facts.text: The applicant was put in a white Renault car with registration number 01 HC 644, which contained two other police officers armed with MP-5 automatic weapons.

anchor.surface_text: On leaving the café the applicant was put in a white Renault car, with the registration number 01 HC 644. There were two other police officers inside the car, both armed with MP-5 automatic weapons.

facts.text: The car drove towards Kabaktepe and stopped in a deserted field where the applicant was taken out and beaten by the police officers with punches, kicks, and gun butts.

anchor.surface_text: The car drove in the direction of Kabaktepe and stopped in a deserted field. The applicant was taken out of the car. As soon as he got out, the police officers started to punch and kick him and to beat him with the butts of their guns.

facts.text: The police officers told the applicant they had seen him at the funeral the day before and threatened him, warning that if he continued such activities, his end would be like the dead HADEP members.

anchor.surface_text: The police officers told the applicant that they had seen him at the funeral of Sefer Cerf and Rehib Çabuk the day before. They threatened him and told him that if he continued to be involved in such activities, his end would be like those of the dead HADEP members.

facts.text: The police officers questioned the applicant about local people and forced him to report on shopkeepers allegedly selling the pro-Kurdish newspaper Özgür Ülke and collecting money for the PKK, threatening to kill him if he did not report regularly.

anchor.surface_text: The police officers questioned the applicant about a number of local people. The applicant was also forced to report the activities of local shopkeepers, who were allegedly selling the newspaper Özgür Ülke, a pro-Kurdish newspaper, and who were collecting money, presumably for the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (hereinafter “the PKK”). The applicant was threatened that if he did not report the political activities of these shopkeepers regularly, he would be killed.

facts.text: The applicant denied involvement in such activities and protested against being treated like a criminal. He was then put back into the car and driven towards town, given an address, and ordered to be there on the following Friday evening.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant denied that he was involved in such activities and protested that they had no reason to treat him like a criminal. He was then put into the car and driven towards the town. Before releasing him, the officers gave the applicant an address and ordered him to be there on the following Friday evening.

facts.text: When the applicant got home, his relatives took him to the hospital where it was established that his jaw bone had been broken and required surgery.

anchor.surface_text: When the applicant got home, his relatives took him to the hospital where it was established that his jaw bone had been broken and required surgery.

facts.text: On 7 October 1994 the applicant, with a lawyer's assistance, submitted a petition to the Adana Prosecutor’s office requesting criminal proceedings against the police officers who had ill-treated him and asked to be sent to the Forensic Medicine Directorate for a medical report.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant, with the assistance of a lawyer, submitted a petition to the Adana Prosecutor’s office on 7 October 1994 and requested the Prosecutor to initiate criminal proceedings against the police officers who had ill-treated him. He gave a detailed account of the incident and described the physical features of the police officers in question. The applicant asked the Prosecutor to send him to the Forensic Medicine Directorate to obtain a medical report which could be used as evidence in the criminal proceedings.

facts.text: A medical report from the Adana Forensic Medicine Directorate on 7 October 1994 concluded the applicant’s left jawbone was broken, not life-threatening, and he was unable to work for 25 days.

anchor.surface_text: The report was obtained from the Adana Forensic Medicine Directorate on 7 October 1994 (for content see paragraph 27 below).

facts.text: The applicant received no replies from the Prosecutor following his petitions.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant received no replies from the Prosecutor.

facts.text: The Adana Public Prosecutor commenced an investigation into the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment on 10 October 1994 under file no. 1994/29324.

anchor.surface_text: On 10 October 1994 the Adana Public Prosecutor commenced an investigation into the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment under file no. 1994/29324.

facts.text: The Adana Prosecutor decided he lacked jurisdiction to prosecute the police officers and forwarded the investigation file to the Adana Administrative Council for authorisation to prosecute.

anchor.surface_text: It appears from this decision that the Adana Prosecutor, after having received the applicant’s petitions, had decided on an unspecified date that he lacked jurisdiction to prosecute the police officers and had forwarded the investigation file to the Adana Administrative Council in order to obtain an authorisation to prosecute the police officers.

facts.text: On 24 November 1994 the Adana Administrative Council found insufficient evidence to open an investigation and declined authorisation to prosecute the four police officers.

anchor.surface_text: On 24 November 1994 the Adana Administrative Council, which was presided over by the deputy Governor of Adana and consisted of six civil servants, found that there was insufficient evidence to open an investigation and decided to decline authorisation for the prosecution of Yaşar Soyyiğit, Hacı Kara, Mustafa Duman and Kadri Dursun, police officers who worked for the anti-terrorism branch of the Adana Police who had allegedly intimidated and ill-treated the applicant on 5 October 1994.

facts.text: On 7 December 1994 the Disciplinary Board of the Adana Police decided not to impose disciplinary measures on the police officers due to lack of evidence.

anchor.surface_text: On 7 December 1994 the Disciplinary Board of the Adana Police decided not to impose any disciplinary measures on the police officers due to a lack of evidence establishing that they had committed the acts complained of.

facts.text: On 31 May 1996 the Council of State quashed the Adana Administrative Council’s decision declining authorisation for prosecution regarding ill-treatment and held the police officers should be tried before the Adana Criminal Court of First Instance.

anchor.surface_text: On 31 May 1996 the Council of State quashed the Adana Administrative Council’s decision declining authorisation for the prosecution of the four police officers in so far as it concerned the offence of ill-treatment and upheld the decision not to grant authorisation to prosecute them for the allegation of intimidation.

facts.text: On 8 August 1996 the Adana Prosecutor forwarded the Council of State decision to the Adana Criminal Court of First Instance and asked the court to take necessary action.

anchor.surface_text: On 8 August 1996 the Adana Prosecutor forwarded the decision to the Adana Criminal Court of First Instance and asked that court to take the necessary action.

facts.text: On 11 August 1996 a preliminary hearing was held before the Ninth Chamber of the Adana Criminal Court of First Instance, which decided to summon the defendants for a hearing on 14 November 1996.

anchor.surface_text: On 11 August 1996 a preliminary hearing was held before the Ninth Chamber of the Adana Criminal Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the trial court”). The court decided to summons the defendants for the next hearing on 14 November 1996 and further decided to obtain the defendants’ identity cards and documents showing their criminal records.

facts.text: On 14 November 1996, only two of the defendants attended the hearing and denied beating the applicant, stating they only checked his identity card and returned it.

anchor.surface_text: On 14 November 1996 the hearing resumed before the trial court. Only two of the defendants, namely Yaşar Soyyiğit and Hacı Kara, were present in the court room. According to postal receipts, the remaining two defendants had also been summonsed. Both Mr Soyyiğit and Mr Kara told the trial court that they had gone to the café on the day in question and checked the identity card of the applicant. When they had established that he was not wanted by the authorities for any offence, they had returned the identity card to the applicant. They had not beaten him up.

facts.text: The trial court sent letters rogatory to courts in other jurisdictions to take statements from the two absent defendants.

anchor.surface_text: The trial court, noting that all defendants except Yaşar Soyyiğit had since been posted elsewhere, decided to send letters rogatory to the courts in whose jurisdiction the two absent defendants were living and asked those courts to take statements from them.

facts.text: On 9 December 1996 and 25 December 1996, the courts taking letters rogatory heard the absent defendants, who denied ill-treatment and claimed the applicant was a PKK member or did not remember the incident.

anchor.surface_text: On 9 December 1996 the Karakoçan Criminal Court of First Instance, acting on the letter rogatory from the trial court, took a statement from Mustafa Duman, one of the two defendants who had failed to attend the hearing before the trial court on 14 November 1996. Mr Duman told the court that neither he nor any of his colleagues had ill-treated the applicant. According to Mr Duman, the applicant had been a PKK member and it was for this reason that he had made the allegations of ill-treatment against the police. On 25 December 1996 the Akçakale Criminal Court of First Instance, also acting on the letter rogatory from the trial court, took a statement from Kadri Dursun, the fourth defendant. Mr Dursun told the court that he did not remember the incident which, in any event, was just an allegation. He did not even know the applicant.

facts.text: During the hearing on 29 January 1997, the applicant and his brother confirmed their statements and the applicant expressed his wish to press charges against the defendants.

anchor.surface_text: During the hearing that was held before the trial court on 29 January 1997, the applicant confirmed the accuracy of the contents of his statement taken at the Police Headquarters previously. He further informed the trial court that he wanted to press charges against the defendants. The applicant’s brother Suphi Dizman also confirmed the accuracy of the contents of his statement taken at the Police Headquarters previously and added that the four police officers had beaten up his brother and broken his jaw as a result.

facts.text: Hearings on 27 March, 4 June and 15 September 1997 were postponed due to failure to submit identity card and criminal records of defendants.

anchor.surface_text: The hearings on 27 March, 4 June and 15 September 1997 had to be postponed on account of the failure of the authorities to submit to the trial court the identity card of Kadri Dursun and the criminal records of Mustafa Duman.

facts.text: On 29 December 1997, the trial court acquitted the defendants, noting their denials and that the medical report was issued two days after the alleged events, concluding insufficient evidence to prove the injury was caused by the defendants.

anchor.surface_text: The trial court, noting that the defendants had “vehemently denied the allegations” against them and taking into account the “fact that the medical report was issued two days after the alleged events”, concluded on 29 December 1997 that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the applicant’s injury had been caused by the defendants, and acquitted them.

anchor.surface_text: Before proceeding to assess the evidence, the Court reiterates that it is of the utmost importance for the effective operation of the system of individual petition instituted under Article 34 of the Convention that States should furnish all necessary facilities to make possible a proper and effective examination of applications (see Tanrıkulu v. Turkey [GC], no. 23763/94, § 70, ECHR 1999-IV). It is inherent in proceedings relating to cases of this nature, where an individual applicant accuses State agents of violating his rights under the Convention, that in certain instances solely the respondent Government have access to information capable of corroborating or refuting these allegations.

precedents.cited_proposition: States must furnish all necessary facilities for effective examination of applications under Article 34 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: It is inherent in proceedings relating to cases of this nature, where an individual applicant accuses State agents of violating his rights under the Convention, that in certain instances solely the respondent Government have access to information capable of corroborating or refuting these allegations. A failure on a Government’s part to submit such information which is in their hands without a satisfactory explanation may not only give rise to the drawing of inferences as to the well-foundedness of the applicant’s allegations, but may also reflect negatively on the level of compliance by a respondent State with its obligations under Article 38 § 1 (a) of the Convention (see Timurtaş v. Turkey, no. 23531/94, §§ 66 and 70, ECHR 2000-VI).

precedents.cited_proposition: Failure to submit information in State's possession may lead to adverse inferences and reflect negatively on compliance with Article 38 § 1 (a).

anchor.surface_text: The same applies to delays by the State in submitting information which prejudices the establishment of the facts in a case (see Orhan v. Turkey, no. 25656/94, § 266, 18 June 2002).

precedents.cited_proposition: Delays by the State in submitting information may prejudice establishment of facts in a case.

anchor.surface_text: The effect of Article 13 is thus to require the provision of a domestic remedy to deal with the substance of an “arguable complaint” under the Convention and to grant appropriate relief, although Contracting States are afforded some discretion as to the manner in which they conform to their Convention obligations under this provision. The scope of the obligation under Article 13 varies depending on the nature of the applicant’s complaint under the Convention. Nevertheless, the remedy required by Article 13 must be “effective” in practice as well as in law, in particular in the sense that its exercise must not be unjustifiably hindered by the acts or omissions of the authorities of the respondent State (see Aksoy v. Turkey, judgment of 18 December 1996, Reports 1996-VI, p. 2286, § 95; Aydın v. Turkey, judgment of 25 September 1997, Reports 1997-VI, pp. 1895-96, § 103; Kaya v. Turkey, judgment of 19 February 1998, Reports 1998-I, § 167).
